parts.title: Carnivorous Plants
parts.article:
Carnivorous plants
 
They attract insects and then eat their flesh. Is that any way for a plant to behave?
 
(A) The naturalist and author of On the Origin of Species, Charles Darwin, was fascinated by carnivorous plants. In 1860, soon after he came across his first carnivorous plant — the sundew, Drosera — he wrote, ‘I care more about Drosera than the origin of all the species in the world.’ He spent months running experiments on the plants. He dropped flies and bits of meat on their leaves and watched them slowly fold their sticky tentacles over their prey. He thought it incredible that brushing a leaf with a single strand of human hair was enough to bring about a response. Yet sundews, he observed, ignored raindrops. To react to such a false alarm, he reasoned, would obviously be a great evil to the plant. This was no accident. This was adaptation.
 
(B) Darwin expanded his studies from sundews to other species in his book Insectivorous Plants. He was amazed at the quickness and power of the Venus flytrap. He showed that when one of its leaves snapped shut, it formed itself into a temporary ‘stomach’, secreting enzymes that could dissolve the prey. He noted that a leaf took more than a week to reopen after closing, and reasoned that the interlocking spines along the margin of the leaf allowed tiny insects to escape, saving the plant the expense of digesting an insufficient meal.
 
(C) Today, biologists using 21st-century tools to study cells and DNA are beginning to understand how these plants hunt, eat, and digest — and how these strange adaptations came about in the first place. Alexander Volkov, a plant physiologist at Oakwood University in Alabama, believes he has figured out the Venus flytrap’s secret. ‘This,’ Volkov declares, ‘is an electrical plant.’ When an insect brushes against a hair on the leaf of a Venus flytrap, the movement sets off an electric charge. The charge builds up inside the tissue of the leaf but is not enough to stimulate the snap, which keeps the Venus flytrap from reacting to false alarms, such as raindrops. An insect, however, is likely to brush a second hair, adding enough electric charge for the leaf to close.
 
(D) Volkov’s experiments reveal that the electric charge travels down fluid-filled tunnels in a leaf, which opens up pores in cell membranes. Water rushes from the cells on the inside of the leaf to those on the outside, causing the leaf to rapidly flip in shape from convex to concave, like a soft contact lens. As the leaves flip, they snap together, trapping an insect inside.
 
(E) The bladderwort plant has an equally sophisticated way of setting its underwater trap. It pumps water out of tiny air sacs or bladders, lowering the pressure inside. When a water flea or some other small creature swims past, it bends hairs on the bladder, causing a flap to spring apart. The low pressure sucks water in, carrying the creature along with it. In one five-hundredth of a second, the flap swings shut again. The cells in the bladder then begin to pump water out again, creating a new vacuum. Many other species of carnivorous plants act like living flypaper, catching animals on sticky tentacles. Pitcher plants use yet another strategy, growing long tube-shaped leaves into which insects fall. Some of the largest have pitchers up to 30cm deep and can consume whole frogs unlucky enough to fall into them. Sophisticated chemistry helps make the pitcher a death trap.
 
(F) Nicholas Gotelli, of the University of Vermont, is trying to figure out what evolutionary forces pushed these plants towards meat. Carnivorous plants clearly benefit from eating animals; when scientists feed pitcher plants extra bugs, the plants get bigger. But the benefits of eating flesh are not the ones you might expect. Carnivorous animals, like ourselves, use the carbon in protein and the fat in meat to build muscles and store energy. Carnivorous plants, however, take nitrogen and phosphorus from the flesh in order to build light-harvesting enzymes. Eating animals, in other words, lets carnivorous plants do what all plants do: grow by taking energy directly from the sun. Unfortunately, they do a really bad job of it. That’s because they have to use a lot of energy to make the equipment they need to catch animals — the enzymes, the pumps, the sticky tentacles, and so on. A pitcher or a flytrap is not very good at photosynthesis because, unlike plants with ordinary leaves, it does not have flat solar panels that can absorb lots of sunlight. Gotelli suspects that only under special conditions are the benefits of being carnivorous greater than the costs. The poor soil of bogs and swamps, where many carnivorous plants grow, offers little nitrogen and phosphorus, so carnivorous plants enjoy an advantage there over ‘conventional’ plants. Also, bogs are often flooded with sunshine, so even an inefficient carnivorous plant can carry out enough photosynthesis to survive. ‘They’re stuck, and they’re making the best of it,’ says Aaron Ellison of Harvard University.
 
(G) Unfortunately, the adaptations that enable carnivorous plants to survive in harsh habitats also make them extremely sensitive to environmental changes. Chemical fertilizers used in agriculture and pollution from power plants are adding extra nitrogen to many bogs in North America. Carnivorous plants are so finely adapted to low levels of nitrogen that this extra fertilizer is overloading their systems. Humans also threaten carnivorous plants in other ways. The black market trade in exotic carnivorous plants is strong, but even if this can be prevented, carnivorous plants will continue to suffer from other dangers. Their habitat is disappearing, to be replaced by shopping centers and houses. The suppression of wildfires by government agencies allows other plants to grow quickly and outcompete the Venus flytraps. Good news, perhaps, for flies. But a loss for all who delight in the inventiveness of evolution.

Questions 1–5
Complete the notes below.
Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes 1–5 on your answer sheet.
Carnivorous Plants
Darwin’s experiments:
Drosera
• He put insects and small amounts of meat onto leaves and observed what happened.
• He was amazed that one human hair triggered a response.
• He understood why the plant did not respond to
Venus flytrap
• He demonstrated how leaves close and then, for a short period, act like a .

Biology today:
Venus flytrap
• If insects come into contact with leaf hairs, their movement produces an electric charge.
• The charge enters fluid-filled tunnels, causing in cell membranes to open.
• Water moves between cells and then the leaf changes from convex to concave, trapping the insect inside.
Bladderwort
• Hairs bend when insects swim past, resulting in the opening of a flap.
• Water is sucked in.
• When water is pumped out of bladder cells, a builds up inside.
Pitcher plants

• Some plants are big enough to capture and eat .
Questions 6–13
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?
In boxes 6–13 on your answer sheet, write:

Q6 Pitcher plants increase in size after they have digested a lot of insects.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q7 Carnivorous plants produce light-harvesting enzymes with the nutrients they extract from animals.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q8 Pitcher plants and Venus flytraps are more efficient at photosynthesis than plants with ordinary leaves.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q9 Venus flytraps are better adapted to the soil of swamps and bogs than other carnivorous plants.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q10 Carnivorous plants frequently find it difficult to photosynthesise in bogs due to a lack of sunlight.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q11 Scientists have campaigned to reduce the amount of nitrogen that is released into the soil by agricultural practices.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q12 A lot of exotic carnivorous plants are sold illegally.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q13 Preventing wildfires is beneficial to the Venus flytrap.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

reference:
Q1

干扰 “Did not respond to” 对应原文的 “ignored”。

句子 (Paragraph A) “Yet sundews, he observed, ignored raindrops. To react to such a false alarm, he reasoned, would obviously be a great evil to the plant.”

解析 题目说达尔文明白了为什么这种植物不对____做出反应，原文A段提到茅膏菜“ignored raindrops（无视雨滴）”，因为这是一种虚假警报，填 raindrops。

Q2

解析 题目说捕蝇草闭合后，在短时间内表现得像一个____，原文B段说它把自己形成一个“temporary stomach（临时的胃）”，填 stomach。

干扰 “Act like” 对应 “formed itself into”，“for a short period” 对应 “temporary”。

句子 (Paragraph B) “...when one of its leaves snapped shut, it formed itself into a temporary ‘stomach’, secreting enzymes that could dissolve the prey.”

Q3

解析 题目说电荷进入充满液体的通道，导致细胞膜上的____打开，原文D段说这打开了细胞膜上的“pores（孔/毛孔）”，填 pores。

干扰 动词 “open” 在原文和题目中一致，定位非常直接。

句子 (Paragraph D) “...electric charge travels down fluid-filled tunnels in a leaf, which opens up pores in cell membranes.”

Q4

干扰 “Builds up inside” 对应原文的 “creating... inside（隐含在语境中）”。

解析 题目说当水被泵出时，内部形成了一个____，原文E段说细胞再次把水泵出，“creating a new vacuum（创造一个新的真空）”，填 vacuum。

句子 (Paragraph E) “The cells in the bladder then begin to pump water out again, creating a new vacuum.”

Q5

解析 题目说有些植物大到足以捕捉并吃掉____，原文E段提到最大的猪笼草可以消耗整只“frogs（青蛙）”，填 frogs。

干扰 “Eat” 对应原文的 “consume”，注意填复数。

句子 (Paragraph E) “Some of the largest have pitchers up to 30cm deep and can consume whole frogs unlucky enough to fall into them.”

Q6

解析 题目说猪笼草在消化大量昆虫后体积会增加。原文F段说当科学家给它们喂额外的虫子时，“the plants get bigger（植物长得更大）”，选 TRUE。

干扰 “Increase in size” 就是 “get bigger” 的同义替换。

句子 (Paragraph F) “...when scientists feed pitcher plants extra bugs, the plants get bigger.”

Q7

句子 (Paragraph F) “Carnivorous plants, however, take nitrogen and phosphorus from the flesh in order to build light-harvesting enzymes.”

干扰 “Nutrients” 概括了原文的 “nitrogen and phosphorus”，“produce” 对应 “build”。

解析 题目说食肉植物利用从动物身上提取的营养制造“捕光酶”。原文F段说它们从肉中摄取氮和磷是为了“build light-harvesting enzymes（制造捕光酶）”，选 TRUE。

Q8

解析 题目说猪笼草和捕蝇草的光合作用效率比普通叶子植物“更高（more efficient）”。原文F段明确说它们“not very good at photosynthesis（不擅长光合作用）”，因为没有平坦的太阳能板，选 FALSE。

干扰 原文是“not very good”，题目是“more efficient”，意思完全相反。

句子 (Paragraph F) “A pitcher or a flytrap is not very good at photosynthesis because, unlike plants with ordinary leaves, it does not have flat solar panels...”

Q9

解析 题目比较捕蝇草和“其他食肉植物”谁更适应沼泽土壤。原文F段只说了食肉植物整体比“传统植物（conventional plants）”有优势，没有在食肉植物内部进行比较，选 NOT GIVEN。

干扰 文中确实提到了适应沼泽，但比较对象是“普通植物”，而非“其他食肉植物”。

句子 (Paragraph F) “...so carnivorous plants enjoy an advantage there over ‘conventional’ plants.”

Q10

句子 (Paragraph F) “Also, bogs are often flooded with sunshine, so even an inefficient carnivorous plant can carry out enough photosynthesis to survive.”

解析 题目说食肉植物在沼泽中因“缺乏阳光（lack of sunlight）”难以进行光合作用。原文F段说沼泽通常“flooded with sunshine（阳光充沛）”，选 FALSE。

干扰 “Flooded with sunshine” 直接反驳了 “lack of sunlight”。

Q11

解析 题目说科学家“发起了运动（campaigned）”以减少农业排放的氮。原文G段只提到化肥增加了氮并导致过载，但没提科学家是否对此发起了抵制运动，选 NOT GIVEN。

干扰 描述了问题（pollution/fertilizers），但未提及解决问题的动作（campaign）。

句子 (Paragraph G) “Chemical fertilizers used in agriculture and pollution from power plants are adding extra nitrogen...”

Q12

解析 题目说大量外来食肉植物被非法出售。原文G段提到外来食肉植物的“black market trade（黑市交易）”很强劲（strong），黑市即非法出售，选 TRUE。

干扰 “Sold illegally” 对应 “black market trade”，“a lot” 对应 “strong”。

句子 (Paragraph G) “The black market trade in exotic carnivorous plants is strong...”

Q13

解析 题目说预防野火对捕蝇草“有益（beneficial）”。原文G段说“suppression of wildfires（抑制野火）”让其他植物生长并“outcompete（竞争过/淘汰）”捕蝇草，这对捕蝇草是有害的，选 FALSE。

干扰 抑制野火（人为干预）反而导致捕蝇草被其他植物挤占生存空间，所以是坏事。

句子 (Paragraph G) “The suppression of wildfires by government agencies allows other plants to grow quickly and outcompete the Venus flytraps.”
